title: Georges Seurat: He Painted a Whole Sunday With Tiny Dots | Born 167 Years Ago Today

lines: He trained at the School of Fine Arts in Paris,
but he also read what scientists wrote about color.
Put two colors side by side, step back,
and they blend inside your eye,
so why not let the viewer's eye do the mixing?
In 1884, he sent his first big painting to the official Salon.
In eighteen eighty-four, he sent his first big painting to the official Salon.
It showed young workers resting by the river; the judges rejected it.
He didn't give up: he and other artists started their own show,
so rejected work could be seen too.

lines: That year, he began painting La Grande Jatte, in the Seine.
That same year, he began painting La Grande Jatte, an island in the Seine.
He went back again and again, made about sixty studies,
and worked on it for two whole years.
The canvas is two meters high and three meters wide,
covered entirely in tiny dots of color.
In 1886, it was shown at the last Impressionist exhibition.
In eighteen eighty-six, it was shown at the last Impressionist exhibition.
A brand-new style, Pointillism, was born,
and later, even Van Gogh tried painting with dots.
In 1891, he died suddenly of illness, at just thirty-one.
In eighteen ninety-one, he died suddenly of illness, at just thirty-one.
In 1924, the Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting.
In nineteen twenty-four, the Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting.
It still hangs there,
and its dots look a lot like the pixels on our screens.
His question for you:
If something took two years to finish, would you keep going?
